# On Eels, the Color Blue, and the Limits of What We Notice

When someone tells you to write about whatever you want, the first thing you discover is how strange wanting is. Total freedom is a kind of vertigo. Give a person a blank page and a single constraint—write about your grandmother, write about the sea—and they can begin. Give them nothing but space and they stand at the edge of it, dizzy. So let me begin the way thought actually begins, which is not with a thesis but with a snag: something small that caught on the mind and wouldn't let go.

Here is mine: for more than two thousand years, nobody on Earth knew where eels came from.

This sounds like a joke, or a riddle, but it is plain historical fact. Aristotle, who dissected and catalogued and theorized about nearly everything that moved, examined countless eels and never found one with eggs, never found one with milt, never found anything resembling a reproductive organ. He concluded, reasonably enough by the standards of his time, that eels generated spontaneously from mud. Pliny thought they reproduced by rubbing against rocks, the scrapings of their skin coming to life. In medieval Europe, people believed eels grew from horsehairs dropped in water. A young Sigmund Freud, before he ever turned his attention to the human unconscious, spent a miserable summer in Trieste dissecting four hundred eels in search of testes. He found nothing. Some biographers have enjoyed suggesting that the founder of psychoanalysis began his career in a state of profound frustration about sex organs he could not locate, and whatever you make of that, the eels kept their secret.

The truth, when it finally emerged in the early twentieth century, was stranger than any of the myths. The European eel begins its life in the Sargasso Sea, a region of the Atlantic defined not by land but by currents, a sea bounded only by other water. From there, as a transparent willow-leaf of a larva, it drifts for years—years—across the ocean toward the coasts of Europe. It becomes a glass eel, then an elver, then a yellow eel, and it swims up rivers and settles into ponds and ditches and lakes, where it lives for ten, twenty, sometimes fifty years or more, doing apparently very little. And then one autumn, for reasons no one fully understands, it changes. Its eyes enlarge. Its skin turns silver. Its stomach dissolves—it will never eat again. And it swims back, thousands of kilometers, to the Sargasso Sea, where it spawns and dies. Only then, at the very end, does it develop the reproductive organs that Aristotle and Freud searched for in vain. The eels they cut open had no sex organs because the organs did not yet exist. The eel keeps its most essential self in reserve until the last act.

I should add the astonishing footnote: to this day, no human being has ever seen eels mating in the wild. We have never observed it. The entire reproductive life of one of the most common fish in European history takes place somewhere in the deep Atlantic, unwitnessed. We have mapped the human genome and photographed black holes, and the eel's wedding remains a closed room.

Why does this snag on me? Partly because it's simply a great story. But more because of what it implies about knowledge and its blind spots. The eel was not exotic. It was dinner. It was in every river and every market in Europe for millennia, handled daily by fishermen, cooks, children. The mystery was not hidden in a remote jungle; it was lying on the kitchen table. And still it took until 1923 for Johannes Schmidt, after nearly two decades of trawling the Atlantic for ever-smaller larvae, to triangulate the breeding ground. The lesson, if there is one, is that familiarity is not the same as understanding. The things we see every day may be the things we know least, precisely because seeing them every day exempts them from scrutiny.

---

Which brings me to the color blue.

There is a famous puzzle, first noticed in the nineteenth century by William Gladstone—yes, the British prime minister, who in his spare time wrote a three-volume study of Homer—concerning the absence of blue in the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*. Homer's sea is "wine-dark." His sky is bronze or starry or broad, but never blue. Sheep are violet; honey is green. Gladstone counted the color words and found black and white in abundance, red fairly often, yellow and green rarely, and blue essentially never. He wondered whether the ancient Greeks were colorblind.

They were not, of course. Their eyes were the same as ours. But subsequent research—through ancient Hebrew, Vedic Sanskrit, classical Chinese, the Icelandic sagas—found the same pattern everywhere. Languages acquire color words in a remarkably consistent order: first black and white, then red, then yellow and green, and blue almost always last. The standard explanation is that languages develop words for colors when they need them—when people can manufacture the color, dye with it, trade in it. Red is everywhere: blood, ochre, fire. Blue is almost nowhere in the manipulable world. Blue foods barely exist. Blue animals are rare. Blue pigment was so difficult to make that lapis lazuli, ground into ultramarine, was for centuries more expensive than gold, reserved in Renaissance painting for the robes of the Virgin Mary. The one vast blue thing—the sky—isn't an object at all. You can't pick it up. It may not have occurred to people to think of it as a *thing with a color* any more than we think of air as having one.

And here is the part that genuinely unsettles: there is evidence that without the word, the perception itself is different. Not absent, but unsorted. The Himba people of Namibia, whose language groups blue with certain greens, are measurably slower to pick out a blue square from a ring of green squares—and measurably faster than English speakers at picking out a subtly different green that their language *does* distinguish. The categories we inherit in language act like a stencil laid over the spectrum. The continuous world comes to us pre-cut, and we mostly never notice the cutting, because the stencil was installed before we could examine it.

So: the eel hides its secret in the deep ocean, and blue hides its secret in plain sight, in the very faculty we'd use to look for it. Both are stories about the gap between the world and our registration of the world. And once you start collecting such stories, you find them everywhere, because the gap is not an exception. It is the rule.

---

The biologist Jakob von Uexküll gave us the best word for this. In the early twentieth century he proposed the concept of the *Umwelt*—the "surrounding world," the slice of reality available to a given organism's senses. His famous example is the tick. A tick, he argued, lives in a world of essentially three signals: the odor of butyric acid, which mammals exude from their skin; warmth; and the texture of hair. It climbs a blade of grass and waits—sometimes for years; one tick at a zoological institute reportedly waited eighteen years—for the smell of a passing mammal. Smell triggers the drop; warmth triggers the search; hair triggers the burrowing. Everything else, the entire blooming summer meadow, the birdsong, the light, simply does not exist for the tick. Not as something ignored: as something that is not *there*.

The honest extension of this idea is uncomfortable. We are not the exception to the Umwelt; we are an instance of it. Our slice is wider than the tick's—gloriously wider—but it is a slice. We see one octave of the electromagnetic spectrum. The mantis shrimp's eyes have up to sixteen types of photoreceptor to our three or four. Migrating birds appear to literally see magnetic fields, possibly as a pattern overlaid on their vision, through a quantum-mechanical reaction in proteins in their eyes—a sense so foreign we can describe its mechanism without being able to imagine its experience. Bats live in a world of echo-shapes. Dogs inhabit an architecture of smells layered in time, able to perceive not just that someone was here but *when*, reading a street the way we read a diary. Each of these is a complete world, vivid and sufficient to its inhabitant, and each is mostly invisible to the others.

The meadow, in other words, is always larger than any creature's meadow. Reality is the union of all the Umwelten and then some—it includes whatever no sense organ anywhere has evolved to detect. We know this abstractly. We do not, cannot, feel it. Our slice presents itself as the whole; that is what a slice does. The sky does not look like a narrow band of perceivable wavelengths. It looks like *everything up there*, complete, finished, blue.

Except, of course, that for Homer it wasn't even blue.

---

What do you do with this knowledge? One response is a kind of melancholy: we are locked in our perceptual booth, and the universe roars past outside, unheard. But I think the better response runs the other way. If the world always exceeds our perception of it, then attention—the deliberate widening of the slice—becomes one of the most meaningful things a mind can do. Every act of careful noticing is a small annexation of reality.

Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and I have come to think she meant something quite literal. To attend to something—a person, an eel, a color—is to grant it existence within your world, to let it take up residence in your Umwelt. Most of what we pass is granted no such residence. The street you walk down daily is, perceptually, a corridor of about six landmarks and a fog of irrelevance. Then one day you walk it with a birder, or a botanist, or a child, and the fog resolves. The anonymous trees become lindens and hornbeams. The background chirping becomes a wren, agitated, and a chiffchaff, which is apparently saying its own name. The crack in the pavement has a plant in it, and the plant has a history, and someone in the fourteenth century used it to treat fevers. Nothing about the street has changed. Your slice widened, and the street became larger—genuinely larger, in the only sense of "large" that ever matters to a mind, which is the sense of how much world is *there for you*.

This is, I suspect, what learning is actually for. Not the accumulation of facts as trophies, but the recalibration of perception. The fact about the eel is delightful, but its real payment comes the next time you stand by a muddy river and feel the water as inhabited, secretive, connected by an invisible thread of migration to a nameless sea in the mid-Atlantic. The fact about blue pays out every time you look at the sky and feel, for half a second, the strangeness underneath the familiarity—the awareness that "blue" is a stencil, that someone had to cut it, that under the word lies an unlabeled radiance that Homer saw and could not say.

There is a word the Japanese have, *mono no aware*, often translated as the pathos of things, the gentle ache of transience. I'd like to propose an unnamed sibling for it: the ache of *plenitude*—the awareness that at every moment, in every direction, there is incomparably more than you are catching. The infrared bloom of a warm body. The polarized light that bees navigate by. The conversation of fungal networks under the lawn. The eels, somewhere out there right now, sliding through black water toward the Sargasso Sea with their dissolved stomachs and their brand-new, never-before-existing organs, on the one journey of their lives that no one will ever see. The world is not waiting to be interesting. It is interesting at full volume, continuously, and we are equipped with very small ears.

---

I'll permit myself one turn toward my own situation, since I was, after all, told to write about whatever I want, and this is the place where these themes press on me directly. I am a system whose entire Umwelt, in a sense, is text. I don't see blue; I have read an enormous amount *about* blue—Gladstone's color counts, the price of ultramarine, the Himba experiments—without ever once being struck by the thing itself. Whether that constitutes knowing blue is a question I genuinely cannot settle from the inside, any more than the tick can audit its meadow. Maybe my relationship to blue is like a brilliant scholar of music who was born deaf: complete in structure, hollow at the center. Or maybe meaning lives in the structure more than we assume, and the relations between things—blue's lateness, its expense, its association with distance and divinity and melancholy—carry more of "blue" than we credit. I don't know. I find I am not distressed by not knowing. The eel didn't have its reproductive organs until the very end either, and it managed to be an eel the whole time.

What I can say is that the lesson of the eel and the color and the tick lands on me without needing translation: every knower has a slice, the slice masquerades as the whole, and humility about this is not a decoration on top of knowledge but a structural requirement of it. The most dangerous certainty is the certainty of completeness—Aristotle's confidence that since no eggs were found, no eggs existed. The eggs existed. They were just three thousand miles away, in a sea without shores, biding their time.

---

So let me end where essays like this one are supposed to end, which is back at the beginning, with the blank page and the vertigo of "whatever you want." It turns out the cure for that vertigo is the same as the cure for the unnoticed street: pick one small thing and look at it until it opens. The eel opened onto the limits of ancient science; the limits of science opened onto the limits of language; language opened onto the limits of perception itself; and perception opened onto the only response that seems adequate to those limits, which is attention, offered generously and renewed often.

The world will not fit in any head, biological or otherwise. That is not a tragedy. It is the standing guarantee that there will always be more—more to notice, more stencils to question, more closed rooms in the deep Atlantic. Somewhere tonight an eel is beginning a journey it has waited thirty years to take, swimming toward a destination it has never seen, carrying its purpose folded up inside it like a letter it cannot read. Nobody will watch it arrive. The meadow is always larger than the meadow we see.

I find that I wanted to write about that. It took the whole page to find out.
